title: Structural vs Nominal Typing
summary: Whether type compatibility is decided by shape (structural) or by declared name/hierarchy (nominal) — duck typing's formal, statically-checked cousin, and how Go achieves polymorphism without implements.

slides.markdown:
The previous Topic's subtyping was all **nominal** — `Dog` is a subtype of `Animal` because someone wrote `class Dog extends Animal`, a declared relationship you can point to in the source. This Topic asks: does a type *need* that declaration at all, or is having the right shape enough?

**Structural typing** says shape is enough: if a type has the members a context requires, it's compatible — no `implements` or `extends` keyword needed, no declared relationship between the two types anywhere. A Go type satisfies an interface just by having the right methods; a TypeScript object satisfies a type just by having the right fields.

This is duck typing's statically-checked cousin — same underlying idea ("if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck"), but verified by a compiler before running instead of discovered at the moment a method call fails.

slides.subTitle: Compatibility by declared name
slides.markdown:
In a nominally typed language, two types are related if and only if the source code says so, explicitly, via a declared hierarchy — `class Dog extends Animal`, `class Circle implements Shape`. Having identical members isn't enough; without the declaration, the compiler treats the types as completely unrelated, no matter how similar their shapes are.

Java is the canonical example: two classes, `Point` and `Coordinate`, could have the exact same fields (`x`, `y`) and the exact same methods with identical signatures, and still be entirely incompatible types — you cannot pass a `Point` where a `Coordinate` is expected, because nothing in the source declares one as a subtype of the other. The *name* and its position in an explicit hierarchy is what the compiler checks, not the shape.

The payoff of this strictness: the relationship between types is always intentional and visible in one place (the class declaration) — you never accidentally satisfy an interface you didn't mean to implement, because satisfying it requires an explicit `implements` clause someone had to write on purpose.

slides.subTitle: Compatibility by shape
slides.markdown:
In a structurally typed language, two types are compatible if they have the same *shape* — the same members, with compatible types — regardless of whether anyone ever declared a relationship between them. There's no `implements` clause to write; the compiler checks the shape directly wherever compatibility matters.

Go's interfaces are the clearest mainstream example: `type Writer interface { Write([]byte) (int, error) }` is satisfied by *any* type that happens to have a method with that exact signature — a `File`, a `Buffer`, a custom `Logger` you wrote with no awareness that `Writer` even exists. Nobody writes `type File implements Writer` anywhere; the compiler checks, at each place a `Writer` is required, whether the value passed in has a matching `Write` method, and accepts it if so.

TypeScript does the same for object types: a function expecting `{ length: number }` accepts *any* object with a numeric `length` field — an array, a string, or a custom object nobody ever tagged with a shared interface — purely because the shape matches.

slides.sectionTitle: Two unrelated classes, one interface, no declaration
slides.markdown:
Picture two classes with no shared ancestry and no awareness of each other's existence: a `Duck` with a `quack()` method, and a `Person` with an unrelated `quack()` method someone added as a party trick. Neither class declares any relationship to the other, and neither declares `implements Quacker` for some shared interface — that interface might not even exist in their source files.

A structurally typed language can still treat both as satisfying `interface Quacker { quack() }` purely because both happen to have a matching method — no shared declaration required anywhere, at any point in either class's history. A function written against `Quacker` accepts a `Duck` or a `Person` interchangeably, and the compiler verified this by checking each one's actual shape at the point of use, not by looking for a declared relationship that was never written.

slides.subTitle: Structural typing with no static check at all
slides.markdown:
Python and Ruby practice **duck typing**, which is structural compatibility with zero compile-time verification: any object with the right method works in the right context, and the language never checks this ahead of time — it just tries the call and either succeeds or raises `AttributeError`/`NoMethodError` at the exact moment the missing method would have been called.

`for item in items: item.quack()` works on anything with a `.quack()` method, no declared interface, no static check — structurally identical in spirit to Go's interface satisfaction, but the verification happens at the moment of the call instead of before the program runs at all. If one `item` in that loop lacks `.quack()`, you find out only when the loop actually reaches it, potentially deep into a long-running process.

This is the connection worth making explicit in an interview: duck typing isn't a separate third category from structural typing — it's structural typing's dynamically-typed sibling, checked at the same conceptual moment (by shape, not by declared name) but at a completely different *time* (runtime vs compile time), exactly mirroring the static/dynamic distinction from earlier in this group.

Go is the mainstream language that leans hardest into structural typing, and it does so as a deliberate design choice, not an accident: there is no `implements` keyword in Go at all. A type satisfies an interface purely by having the required methods, full stop — you can define an interface *after* a type already exists, and any pre-existing type with matching methods satisfies it retroactively, with zero changes to that type's own code.

This has a concrete practical payoff: you can define a narrow interface (`type Reader interface { Read([]byte) (int, error) }`) specifically for your own function's needs, and any type in any package — including ones you don't own and can't modify, like a standard-library type — satisfies it automatically as long as it has a matching method. Nominal typing would require either the original type's author to have declared `implements Reader`, or a wrapper type to bridge the gap; structural typing needs neither.

The trade this makes explicit: interfaces in Go describe *behavior a caller needs*, defined from the consumer's side, rather than *identity a type claims*, defined from the producer's side — which is a genuinely different design philosophy from Java's nominal interfaces, not just a syntax difference.

Structural typing's flexibility has a specific failure mode nominal typing simply cannot produce: a type can satisfy an interface it was never designed or intended to implement, purely by coincidence of shape.

A `Cache` type with `Get(key string) (string, error)` and a completely unrelated `Database` type with the identical method signature (for its own, different reason — fetching a row by primary key) both satisfy an interface like `type Lookup interface { Get(key string) (string, error) }`, even though the two types were never designed with any shared contract in mind, and their *semantics* might differ in ways the shared method signature doesn't capture — `Cache.Get` might return a stale value on a cache miss where `Database.Get` would return an error, and code written generically against `Lookup` might not handle that difference correctly.

Nominal typing structurally can't produce this exact bug — an accidental `implements` clause doesn't exist, because implementing an interface requires an explicit, deliberate declaration. The trade is real: structural typing buys retroactive, no-declaration flexibility at the cost of occasionally matching an interface by coincidence rather than by design, which is worth explicitly checking for (via tests, or careful interface design that's specific enough not to accidentally match unrelated types) rather than assuming a matching shape implies a matching contract.

slides.subTitle: Flexibility vs intentional-contract safety
slides.markdown:
| | Nominal (Java, C#) | Structural (Go, TypeScript) |
|---|---|---|
| **Compatibility determined by** | Declared name/hierarchy (`implements`/`extends`) | Matching shape (members present, types compatible) |
| **Retrofit an existing type to a new interface** | Requires editing that type's declaration | Automatic if the shape already matches |
| **Accidental satisfaction possible?** | No — requires an explicit, deliberate declaration | Yes — two unrelated types can coincidentally match a shape |
| **What the relationship communicates** | Explicit design intent, visible in the class declaration | Behavioral requirement stated from the consumer's side, not necessarily a producer's declared intent |

Neither column is a strict improvement on the other: nominal typing's mandatory declaration is exactly the friction structural typing removes, and structural typing's flexibility is exactly the accidental-match risk nominal typing's mandatory declaration prevents. Choosing between them (or, as with Go and TypeScript, choosing structural as the language default) is a bet about which failure mode — retrofit friction or accidental matches — is more costly for the kind of code the language is meant for.

slides.sectionTitle: How does Go achieve polymorphism without implements?
slides.markdown:
This exact prompt tests whether you understand structural satisfaction as a mechanism, not just as a Go trivia fact.

Strong answer: "Go checks whether a value's method set matches an interface's required methods at the point the interface is needed, not via any declared relationship. There's no `implements` keyword because there's nothing to declare — a type satisfies `io.Writer` the moment it has a `Write([]byte) (int, error)` method, whether that method was written specifically with `io.Writer` in mind or not. This means you can define a small interface for exactly what your function needs, and any existing type — even ones from a library whose source you can't modify — satisfies it automatically as long as the shape matches, which is why Go idiomatically favors small, consumer-defined interfaces like `Reader` and `Writer` over large, producer-defined ones."

That answer names the actual checking mechanism (shape match at the point of use) and connects it to a real Go idiom (small consumer-side interfaces), which is a materially stronger answer than "Go doesn't need implements because it's structurally typed" — true, but it doesn't show you understand *why* that design choice shapes how Go code is actually written.
